observations.title: CSV file encoding handling in rows_from_file function
observations.subtitle: io.TextIOWrapper decodes CSV files with configurable encoding before csv.DictReader processing
observations.facts: ["rows_from_file function at line 288 in sqlite_utils/utils.py accepts dialect parameter for csv.DictReader","At line 349, decoded_fp wraps file pointer using io.TextIOWrapper with use_encoding parameter","csv.DictReader processes the text-wrapped file pointer starting at line 351-353","csv.field_size_limit is managed with ORIGINAL_CSV_FIELD_SIZE_LIMIT backup at line 53","Function supports encoding parameter passed through to file decoding and dialect detection"]
observations.narrative: The rows_from_file function in sqlite_utils/utils.py handles CSV file reading by wrapping the input file pointer with io.TextIOWrapper using a configurable encoding parameter. The csv.DictReader then operates on this text-wrapped file. The encoding used in the TextIOWrapper is critical for BOM handling - if use_encoding is 'utf-8' rather than 'utf-8-sig', the UTF-8 BOM (0xEF 0xBB 0xBF) would not be automatically stripped. The function also manages CSV field size limits and supports dialect detection via csv.Sniffer.

observations.title: sqlite-utils defaults to utf-8-sig encoding for CSV, which automatically strips UTF-8 BOM
observations.subtitle: Line 349 sets use_encoding default to "utf-8-sig" unless explicit encoding specified, handling BOM transparently
observations.facts: ["rows_from_file function at line 288 accepts optional encoding parameter (defaults to None)","Line 349: `use_encoding: str = encoding or \"utf-8-sig\"` - uses utf-8-sig as default encoding","utf-8-sig encoding in Python's io.TextIOWrapper automatically strips UTF-8 BOM (0xEF 0xBB 0xBF)","BOM stripping applies whenever format=Format.CSV or when format is auto-detected as CSV","User can override with explicit encoding parameter, but utf-8-sig is the standard default"]
observations.narrative: The sqlite-utils rows_from_file function automatically handles UTF-8 BOM in CSV files by defaulting to the utf-8-sig encoding when reading CSV/TSV data. When a BinaryIO file object is wrapped with io.TextIOWrapper at line 349, the encoding parameter defaults to "utf-8-sig" unless the caller explicitly provides a different encoding. The utf-8-sig codec in Python automatically detects and removes the UTF-8 BOM (Byte Order Mark) that some CSV exporters prepend to files. This means users do not need to manually strip the BOM - it is handled transparently by default. If a user does pass encoding='utf-8' explicitly, the BOM would not be stripped, but this is not the default behavior.

observations.title: sqlite-utils plugin discovery mechanism
observations.subtitle: sqlite-utils uses pluggy with setuptools entry points for plugin discovery via "sqlite_utils" namespace
observations.facts: ["Plugin system is implemented in sqlite_utils/plugins.py using the pluggy library","Hook specifications are defined in sqlite_utils/hookspecs.py and registered with the PluginManager","Plugin discovery happens lazily via pm.load_setuptools_entrypoints(\"sqlite_utils\")","Plugins must register as setuptools entry points with the \"sqlite_utils\" namespace to be discovered","get_plugins() function returns list of loaded plugins with their names, versions, and hook names","Plugin loading is skipped during test runs (when sys._called_from_test is set)"]
observations.narrative:
sqlite-utils discovers plugins using pluggy, a plugin framework by pytest. The discovery mechanism works by:

1. Creating a PluginManager in plugins.py with namespace "sqlite_utils"
2. Registering hook specifications from the hookspecs.py module
3. Using lazy loading - plugins are only discovered when ensure_plugins_loaded() is called
4. Calling pm.load_setuptools_entrypoints("sqlite_utils") to load plugins registered as setuptools entry points

This means external packages like sqlite-utils-geo must register themselves as setuptools entry points with the "sqlite_utils" group to be discovered. The hook specs in hookspecs.py define the available hook points that plugins can implement.

observations.title: sqlite-utils plugin hook specifications
observations.subtitle: Two main hooks available for plugins: register_commands for CLI extension and prepare_connection for SQLite customization
observations.facts: ["Hook specifications are defined in sqlite_utils/hookspecs.py using pluggy's HookspecMarker","register_commands() hook allows plugins to add custom CLI commands to the sqlite-utils command group","prepare_connection() hook allows plugins to modify SQLite connections (e.g., register custom SQL functions)","Both hookspec and hookimpl markers use the \"sqlite_utils\" namespace","Hook specifications are defined as simple function signatures with docstrings describing their purpose"]
observations.narrative:
The sqlite-utils plugin system defines two main extension points via hookspecs.py:

1. **register_commands(cli: click.Group)** - Plugins can implement this to register additional CLI commands that extend the sqlite-utils command-line interface.

2. **prepare_connection(conn: sqlite3.Connection)** - Plugins can implement this to customize SQLite connections, such as registering custom SQL functions or setting pragmas.

These hook specifications form the contract between sqlite-utils and plugins. External plugins like sqlite-utils-geo would implement one or both of these hooks to extend functionality.

observations.title: CLI sampling strategy: establish order by random() approach and mutual exclusivity
observations.subtitle: Confirmed implementation approach for --sample flag based on prior testing; random-offset method rejected due to duplicates and WITHOUT ROWID incompatibility.
observations.facts: ["Random-offset approach (offset abs(random()) % count) returns duplicate rows and fails for WITHOUT ROWID tables","Recommended implementation: order by random() limit N","CLI flag design: --sample and --order must be mutually exclusive with error if both provided"]
observations.narrative: Prior experimentation with random-offset sampling for --sample flag revealed fundamental limitations: duplicate row returns and incompatibility with WITHOUT ROWID table definitions. Implementation requirement established to use order by random() limit N instead, which avoids these issues. CLI interface design decision made to prevent --sample and --order flags from being used together, requiring error handling when both flags are specified simultaneously.

observations.title: TypeTracker uses ValueTracker to evaluate column types with test_integer and test_float methods
observations.subtitle: TypeTracker wraps iterators, evaluating each value through ValueTracker test methods in precedence order.
observations.facts: ["TypeTracker.wrap() iterates through rows and calls ValueTracker.evaluate() for each value in each column","ValueTracker maintains couldbe dictionary with test functions for different types (test_integer, test_float, etc.)","ValueTracker.test_integer() uses int() casting with try/except to detect integer types","ValueTracker.test_float() uses float() casting with try/except to detect float types","guessed_type property returns type based on precedence order from get_tests() method","ValueTracker.evaluate() method called for each value to filter out impossible types","TypeTracker stores ValueTracker instances in self.trackers dictionary keyed by column name"]
observations.narrative: User examined TypeTracker implementation to understand the type detection mechanism. TypeTracker wraps an iterator of dictionaries and for each row, creates or retrieves a ValueTracker instance for each column key. ValueTracker uses test methods (test_integer, test_float, etc.) to evaluate whether each value could be a particular type. Type casting is attempted using int() and float() functions with exception handling. The evaluate() method filters out type possibilities as values are processed. The guessed_type property returns the final type based on precedence order defined in get_tests(). This is the core mechanism handling per-column type guessing during CSV import.

observations.subtitle: Implemented random row sampling using order by random() limit N with mutual exclusivity validation.
observations.facts: ["Added keyword-only sample parameter to Queryable.rows_where() method","sample parameter accepts int | None, defaults to None","Validation raises ValueError if sample is combined with order_by, limit, or offset parameters","When sample is not None, appends \"order by random() limit {sample}\" to SQL query","Original order_by/limit/offset logic preserved when sample is None","Docstring updated documenting sample parameter and constraint against combining with order_by, limit, offset"]
observations.narrative: Implemented sampling feature in rows_where() method using "order by random() limit N" SQL pattern. Added keyword-only sample parameter that accepts an integer row count. When sample is specified, the method generates SQL with random ordering and limit clause instead of using provided order_by/limit/offset parameters. Validation ensures sample cannot be used simultaneously with order_by, limit, or offset—attempting to do so raises ValueError. Original behavior preserved when sample is None, maintaining backward compatibility. This implements the established design decision to avoid random-offset approach which returns duplicates and fails on WITHOUT ROWID tables.

observations.title: ValueTracker.evaluate() returns early for falsy values including zero
observations.subtitle: evaluate() method skips type testing when value is falsy or couldbe is empty, potentially affecting zero values.
observations.facts: ["ValueTracker.evaluate() method has early return: `if not value or not self.couldbe: return`","Early return condition treats zero (0) as falsy, skipping type testing for zero values","When early return occurs, no type tests are run and couldbe dictionary is not updated","Type narrowing via del self.couldbe[key] only happens if early return is not triggered","This affects any value that evaluates as falsy: 0, empty string, None, False, etc."]
observations.narrative: User examined ValueTracker.evaluate() method implementation. The method has an early return guard: `if not value or not self.couldbe: return`. This means if a value is falsy (including the integer 0), the method returns immediately without running any type tests. This prevents the couldbe dictionary from being updated for that value. For a column containing a zero value, this early return would skip type testing, potentially causing the column's type detection to be incorrect or underdetermined. This could be the source of the type detection bug affecting integer values, particularly those that are zero or other falsy values.

observations.title: SpatiaLite loading mechanism in sqlite-utils and Lambda constraints
observations.subtitle: User investigating SpatiaLite extension discovery mechanism in sqlite-utils amid production deployment constraints.
observations.facts: ["Ingest database schema freeze deadline: 2026-11-01","SpatiaLite extension cannot be shipped to production due to Lambda layer size limit","User investigating where and how sqlite-utils looks for or loads the SpatiaLite extension"]
observations.narrative: User is investigating how sqlite-utils discovers and loads the SpatiaLite spatial database extension. This discovery is prompted by a production deployment constraint: the SpatiaLite extension cannot be included in Lambda layer deployments due to size limits. Understanding where sqlite-utils attempts to find SpatiaLite will inform whether runtime/optional loading is possible or if alternatives are needed for spatial query functionality.

observations.title: SpatiaLite extension discovery mechanism in sqlite-utils
observations.subtitle: sqlite-utils searches hardcoded paths for mod_spatialite shared library during SpatiaLite initialization.
observations.facts: ["find_spatialite() function defined at line 102 of sqlite_utils/utils.py searches for SpatiaLite extension","SPATIALITE_PATHS tuple at line 44 contains five hardcoded search paths: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/mod_spatialite.so, /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/mod_spatialite.so, /usr/local/lib/mod_spatialite.dylib, /usr/local/lib/mod_spatialite.so, /opt/homebrew/lib/mod_spatialite.dylib","find_spatialite() iterates SPATIALITE_PATHS and returns path to first existing mod_spatialite library or None if none found","Extension can be loaded via db.init_spatialite(find_spatialite()) or db.conn.enable_load_extension(True) + db.conn.load_extension(path)"]
observations.narrative: sqlite-utils uses a hardcoded search strategy for locating the SpatiaLite spatial database extension. The find_spatialite() function looks for mod_spatialite shared libraries in standard system library paths, covering Linux (both x86_64 and aarch64 architectures), macOS (both /usr/local and Homebrew paths), and falls back to None if not found. This fixed set of paths explains why SpatiaLite cannot be easily bundled in Lambda layer deployments—it must be installed in one of these standard system locations, and Lambda layer size constraints make this difficult. For production use where SpatiaLite is not available in standard system paths, alternative approaches such as using db.execute() for spatial queries or relying on application-side spatial processing would be necessary.
